hub.description: Decks and fences for Murfreesboro, TN homes, planned around HOA rules, heavy clay, and the limestone sitting close to the surface in many yards.
hub.intro: Murfreesboro has grown fast, and a lot of that growth came as new subdivisions where the house was finished but the backyard was not. You may have a back door with nothing under it but a couple of stepping stones, or a lot line with no fence and a neighbor's patio in full view. Other Murfreesboro homeowners have the opposite problem: a deck or fence that has stood for a long time and is starting to give out. Below is what shapes both jobs here, with links to the deck and fence pages for more.

sections.heading: What a Murfreesboro backyard usually starts with
paragraphs: In a newer Murfreesboro neighborhood, the yard you bought was shaped by the home builder. The grading was set to push rain away from the foundation and toward a swale, often along the back or side lot line. The soil right next to the house is backfill, which is looser than the ground farther out. Sod or seed went down over whatever was left once construction wrapped up. None of that is a problem, but it matters. A deck footing or a fence line that ignores the swale can send water somewhere it was never meant to go.

In older parts of Murfreesboro the starting point is different. Trees have had decades to grow, roots run close to the surface, and the deck out back was built to whatever standard applied when the house went up. Replacing it is often more about safety than looks. New house or old, in Westfork, The Knolls, or anywhere else in town, the first job is the same. Walk the yard and watch where water runs in a storm. Then find the property corners.

sections.heading: Rock and clay under Murfreesboro yards
paragraphs: Much of Rutherford County sits on limestone, and in a lot of Murfreesboro yards it is close to the surface. The cedar glades around the county are a sign of it: open patches of thin soil over flat limestone, ringed by red cedars. Where the soil is deeper, it tends to be clay that holds water after a hard rain and cracks as summer dries it out. For a deck, that means footings have to be planned around what the digging turns up. For a fence, it means post holes that stop short on rock and posts that sit in wet ground. Ask any contractor you talk to how they handle both, and how rock shows up in the price.

sections.heading: Decks for Murfreesboro homes
paragraphs: A good Murfreesboro deck starts at the back door. On many houses that door sits a few steps above the yard, so even a simple deck needs stairs and railings plus a solid connection to the house. Then comes the sun. A deck facing west takes the full afternoon heat through a Tennessee summer, which affects the boards you choose and whether you want shade. Our page for [deck builder work in Murfreesboro](/deck-builder-murfreesboro-tn/) goes deeper on footings in rocky ground and on replacing an old deck that has gone soft.

sections.heading: Fences for Murfreesboro lots
paragraphs: For most Murfreesboro homeowners, a fence is about privacy or a dog, and often both. Lots in newer subdivisions tend to sit close together, so a privacy fence along the back and sides can make a patio feel like your own again. The catch is that if you have an HOA, it likely has a say in the style and height, and maybe in which side faces out. Rock in the post holes and a drainage swale along the back line also need a plan. The page on [fence installation in Murfreesboro](/fence-company-murfreesboro-tn/) covers property lines and setting posts in wet clay, plus fencing for dogs.

sections.heading: HOA approval and city or county rules
paragraphs: Plenty of Murfreesboro subdivisions have an HOA with an architectural review step, and it usually has to approve a deck or fence before any work starts. Covenants often cover materials and colors, and many limit how far forward a fence can run toward the street. Get the current rules in writing from your management company, because older copies passed around the neighborhood may be out of date. Our guide to [getting HOA approval for a fence or deck](/guides/hoa-approval-deck-fence/) walks through putting a clean submission together.

Separate from the HOA, there are city and county rules. A Murfreesboro mailing address does not always mean the house is inside city limits. Some homes with that address sit in unincorporated Rutherford County, which has its own codes office. If your lot backs up to the Stones River or one of its forks, part of it may sit in a mapped floodplain, which can bring extra review. Rules vary and change, so confirm with the right office before anything goes in the ground.

sections.heading: Before you ask for a price
paragraphs: An estimate is only as good as what goes into it. Before you reach out, find your plat or survey, the HOA rules, and some photos of the back of the house and the yard. Think about how you want to use the space, such as where the grill goes and whether the mower needs a wide gate. If you want both a deck and a fence, say so up front, since the order of the work matters. When you are ready, use the [estimate form](#estimate) and tell us what you have in mind for your Murfreesboro yard.

faqs.q: Should I build the deck or the fence first?
faqs.a: In many Murfreesboro yards the deck goes first. Deck work brings in lumber and concrete, and sometimes digging equipment, and all of that is easier to get to the back of the house before a fence closes the yard off. Building the deck first also lets you place fence gates where the deck stairs actually land. If the fence is urgent because of a dog or a pool, it can go first with a wide gate planned for access.

faqs.q: Does my Murfreesboro HOA have to approve a deck or fence?
faqs.a: If your Murfreesboro neighborhood has an HOA, the answer is usually yes. Covenants commonly require approval for any exterior change you can see from the street or a neighbor's yard. Decks and fences both qualify. Submit before you sign a contract or set a start date, because tearing out a fence the HOA turned down costs far more than waiting. Your management company can send the current form and rules.

faqs.q: Will rock in my Murfreesboro yard stop the project?
faqs.a: Almost never. Limestone near the surface is common around Murfreesboro and across Rutherford County, and it changes how the work gets done, not whether it gets done. Holes that hit rock may need a different tool, a shifted location, or another way of anchoring that meets code. What you want from any builder is a clear answer on how rock is handled and priced before the job starts, so there are no surprises halfway through.

deck.description: Deck builder in Murfreesboro, TN for new construction lots and old deck replacements, with footings planned around rock, clay, and HOA review.
deck.intro: If you live in Murfreesboro, whether in Blackman or Salem Creek, there is a good chance your back door opens onto a drop, a small concrete pad, or a strip of sod that turns to mud after every storm. Maybe the house is new and the builder never added a deck. Maybe the deck that came with an older house is showing its age. Either way, the same questions come up before anyone digs. What is under this yard? What will the HOA allow? How do you know a bid covers everything it should?

sections.heading: Footings in Murfreesboro rock and clay
paragraphs: A deck is only as solid as the footings under its posts, and footings are where Murfreesboro ground causes trouble. Limestone runs close to the surface across much of Rutherford County. One hole can reach full depth while the next one, a few feet away, stops on flat rock. Where there is soil, it is usually dense clay that stays wet in spring and shrinks and cracks as it dries in late summer. Neither one is a reason to skip the deck. Both are reasons to plan the footings before anyone orders framing lumber.

When a footing hole hits rock, there are honest options. A post can often slide a little along the beam without changing the design. Solid rock can itself become the bearing surface, with the footing pinned to it in a way the inspector accepts. On some decks, longer beam spans mean fewer footings to dig. What should never happen is a post set on loose dirt over rock because the hole got hard to dig. Ask any deck builder you are considering how they have handled this before.

sections.heading: New construction houses in Murfreesboro
paragraphs: If your home is part of the newer growth around Murfreesboro, a few things about it matter for a deck. The ground right next to the foundation is backfill, dirt pushed back in after the foundation went up. It is looser than the undisturbed soil farther out, so footings near the house need to go past it to reach firm ground. Where the deck ledger attaches, the siding has to come off so the ledger can bolt to the rim of the house and be flashed properly. Bolting through siding and hoping caulk keeps the water out is how rot starts.

The builder's grading plan matters too. New lots are shaped to move water away from the house and along swales toward the street or a drain. A deck can usually sit over that flow, but skirting packed tight to the ground, or a patio poured underneath, can dam it. Before you settle on a deck size, find out where the water goes in a hard rain. A few minutes out back during a storm tells you more than any drawing.

sections.heading: HOA and permit steps for a Murfreesboro deck
paragraphs: Plenty of Murfreesboro neighborhoods have an HOA, and most will want to see the deck plans before anything is built. Many ask for a site plan showing where the deck sits on the lot and a simple drawing with dimensions. Some also want the material and stain color. Some review committees meet on a set schedule, so a submission that misses one meeting waits for the next. Plan around that if you want it done by summer.

Permits are a separate step. Inside city limits, the City of Murfreesboro lists decks among the projects that need a permit, and inspections generally start with the footing holes before concrete goes in. Outside city limits, the Rutherford County building codes office handles permits. Rules vary and change, so check with the office that covers your address. Our guide to [deck permits in Tennessee](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains the general process and why unpermitted work can cause headaches when you sell.

sections.heading: Choosing boards for Tennessee sun and humidity
paragraphs: Pressure treated pine is still a common decking choice around Middle Tennessee. It costs less up front, and a single bad board is easy to swap. The tradeoff is upkeep. In humid summers it can grow mildew in the shade, and in full sun it checks and splits faster if it is not sealed on a regular schedule. Composite boards skip the staining and resist rot, but they cost more and can get hot underfoot on a deck that faces west in July.

The right answer depends on your yard more than on a brochure. A deck shaded by mature trees stays cooler but also stays damp longer. A bare new construction lot in Murfreesboro, with no trees yet, gets sun all afternoon. Our comparison of [wood vs composite decking](/guides/wood-vs-composite-decking/) covers upkeep and surface heat for Tennessee weather.

sections.heading: Replacing an old deck in Murfreesboro
paragraphs: Not every project starts with a bare yard. Plenty of Murfreesboro homes have a deck that has been through a lot of Tennessee summers. Gray deck boards and peeling stain are cosmetic. The things to worry about are underneath: a ledger with no flashing and dark rot behind it, posts buried in soil instead of sitting on footings, rusted hangers, and railings that move when you lean on them. If more than one of those shows up, replacing usually makes more sense than patching.

Tearing out the old deck is part of the job, so it should be in the bid. So should hauling it away, checking the house wall where the old ledger was, and fixing any rot in the rim before the new ledger goes on. A new deck on the same footprint may still need a permit, and the old footings may need to be redone to meet current rules.

sections.heading: Sizing a deck for the way you use the yard
paragraphs: Lots in many Murfreesboro subdivisions sit close together, so a raised deck can put you face to face with the neighbor's kitchen window. A two level deck, with the lower part stepping down toward the grass, can feel more private than one big platform at door height. Leave room for a table with the chairs pulled out, plus a clear path from the door to the stairs. If privacy is the bigger worry, a stretch of fence may help more than a bigger deck, and our [Murfreesboro fence page](/fence-company-murfreesboro-tn/) covers that side.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to build a deck in Murfreesboro?
faqs.a: Inside city limits, yes. The City of Murfreesboro lists decks among the projects that need a permit. Outside city limits, Rutherford County has its own building codes office, so call the county to ask what your deck needs. A good deck builder will tell you up front whether a permit is needed and who is pulling it. If someone suggests skipping it to save time, treat that as a warning sign.

faqs.q: How is rock priced when deck footings are dug in Murfreesboro?
faqs.a: It varies by contractor, so ask before you sign. Some build an allowance for rock into the bid. Others price the job for normal digging and charge for extra time or equipment if they hit a shelf. Neither approach is wrong, but you should know which one you are agreeing to. Around Murfreesboro, assuming there will be no rock at all is the riskier bet.

faqs.q: Should I wait for my new house to settle before adding a deck?
faqs.a: There is no need to wait on the house itself, but the yard around it matters. Fresh backfill near the foundation keeps settling for a while, which is why footings need to reach undisturbed soil below it. If the lot is still bare, letting the grading and sod take hold through a rainy season shows you where water runs. If your home builder is still handling repair requests, ask whether adding a deck changes anything.

faqs.q: I own a rental near MTSU. What kind of deck makes sense there?
faqs.a: For a Murfreesboro rental near Middle Tennessee State University, simple and sturdy usually wins. Pick straightforward stairs and railings, framing that is easy to look over, and boards you can replace one at a time. Decks on rentals see heavy use, so check railings and stair treads every time the unit turns over. A permitted, inspected deck matters even more on a rental, since other people use it every day.

faqs.q: How do I compare deck bids in Murfreesboro?
faqs.a: Line the bids up and look past the total. Check whether each one spells out the footing plan, how the ledger attaches and gets flashed, the board and railing materials, the stairs, and removal of anything old. Look for how rock is handled and who pulls the permit. A much lower number often leaves one of those out. Our guide on [what drives deck cost](/guides/deck-cost-middle-tennessee/) explains the rest.

fence.description: Fence installation in Murfreesboro, TN: privacy fences for HOA subdivisions, posts set for rock and clay, and property lines checked before digging.
fence.intro: Whether you live in Salem Creek or on an older street near downtown, a fence in Murfreesboro usually has a job to do. Maybe the dog needs to stay in the yard. Maybe you are tired of looking at three other patios from your own, or you want a clear line where your lot ends. The work sounds simple enough, a row of posts and some boards, but Rutherford County ground and neighborhood rules add steps that are easy to miss. Here is what matters before the first fence post goes in.

sections.heading: Setting fence posts in Murfreesboro ground
paragraphs: Posts carry the whole fence, and in Murfreesboro they have to deal with two kinds of ground. In one spot the auger finds limestone a short way down, sometimes a solid shelf and sometimes loose chunks mixed into the clay. In another it cuts through heavy clay that stays wet for days after a spring storm. A post left shallow because the hole hit rock can start to tip once strong wind pushes on a solid privacy fence. One sitting in a cup of wet clay can rot at the ground line long before the boards wear out.

Rock can be drilled, and it is worth paying for instead of cutting posts short. Sometimes a post can move along the line to miss a shelf, as long as the spacing still works for the fence panels. For wet clay, the answer is drainage at the bottom of the hole and concrete shaped so water runs away from the post instead of pooling against it. When you get a price for fence installation in Murfreesboro, ask how rock is handled and whether drilling is included or billed separately.

sections.heading: Privacy fences and HOA rules in Murfreesboro
paragraphs: In many Murfreesboro subdivisions, lots are tight and backyards often face each other, so a privacy fence is often the biggest change you can make to how the yard feels. It is also the change an HOA is most likely to regulate. Covenants often set the style and height, the stain color, and how far toward the street the fence can run. Many require the finished side to face out. Read your covenants and get approval in writing before any fence company orders material.

Within those rules, Murfreesboro homeowners usually still have choices. A board on board fence blocks the view from every angle. Shadowbox lets some air through and looks the same from both sides, which the neighbors tend to like. Horizontal boards give a cleaner look, but long runs need careful framing to keep boards from sagging. Our guide to [privacy fence options](/guides/privacy-fence-options/) compares these fence styles for Tennessee wind and weather.

sections.heading: Property lines, pins, and drainage swales
paragraphs: New construction in Murfreesboro makes property lines harder to find than you would think. The pins set at your lot corners can end up buried under sod, knocked loose by equipment, or pulled up during grading. Do not go by where the grass changes or where the neighbor stops mowing. Find your plat, look for the pins with a metal detector, and if they are gone, have a surveyor mark the corners. Being a few feet off can start an argument that lasts as long as the fence does.

Subdivision plats also show easements, often for drainage or utilities along the back or side lines. In many subdivisions, a swale along the rear of the lot carries water from several yards at once. Fencing can usually cross it, but the bottom has to leave room for water to pass, and some plats or HOAs limit what goes inside an easement. Call Tennessee 811 before digging so buried utility lines get marked. Our guide to [fences and property lines in Tennessee](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) also covers the talk with your neighbor.

sections.heading: How wood holds up in Murfreesboro weather
paragraphs: Murfreesboro summers run hot and humid, and winters bring enough freezing and thawing to work on anything set in the ground. On a newer lot with no shade trees, a wood fence feels all of it. Boards shrink and swell, stain fades fastest on the sides facing south and west, and the bottoms of pickets stay damp where they sit close to the grass. A few habits help a lot. Keep the bottom edge of the boards off the dirt. Do not let mulch or soil pile against posts. Stain or seal once the new wood has dried enough to take it.

sections.heading: Keeping dogs in and meeting pool rules
paragraphs: If the fence is mostly for a dog, think like the dog. Diggers go under, and Murfreesboro clay after a rain is soft enough to make that easy, so a buried strip of wire or a board along the bottom helps. Jumpers need a taller fence. Climbers need a side with no rails to use as a ladder. On sloped ground, close the gaps that open up under each section. Gates are the weak spot, so use latches that close on their own and hinges stout enough to keep the gate from sagging. Our guide on the [best fence for dogs](/guides/best-fence-for-dogs/) goes further.

Pools bring their own rules. A pool enclosure, or a yard fence that doubles as a pool barrier, has rules on height and gate hardware, plus the size of any openings, and they vary by jurisdiction. Confirm them with the Murfreesboro or Rutherford County codes office before you pick a style, since a barrier that fails inspection has to be redone.

sections.heading: What to ask a fence company in Murfreesboro
paragraphs: Before you sign a fence contract, get a few answers in writing. Who calls 811, and who handles the permit if one is needed? Has the HOA approved the exact style listed on the bid? Where do the gates go, and how wide are they? What happens to the dirt and rock that come out of the post holes? A crew that answers those clearly has thought about your yard and not just the length of the fence line. If a deck is also on your list, mention it now, since the order of the work matters. The [Murfreesboro deck builder page](/deck-builder-murfreesboro-tn/) explains why.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a fence in Murfreesboro?
faqs.a: It depends on where you live. Inside city limits, the City of Murfreesboro requires a permit for a residential fence. In unincorporated Rutherford County, the county does not require a building permit for a fence, but it does ask for a fence affidavit with its planning department before work starts. Pool barriers have their own rules. Rules change, so check with the right office. HOA approval is a separate step and does not replace either one.

faqs.q: Which side of the fence should face my neighbor?
faqs.a: Many HOAs in Murfreesboro require the finished side to face out, toward the neighbor or the street. Posts and rails stay on your side. Even without a rule, that is the neighborly choice, and it usually looks better from the road. A shadowbox style looks finished from both sides, if that matters to you. Whatever you pick, tell the neighbor before the crew shows up. A short conversation now saves a lot of awkward ones later.

faqs.q: Can my fence cross the drainage swale behind my house?
faqs.a: Usually, but carefully. Check your plat for a drainage easement and read your HOA rules. Inside city limits, a fence in a drainage easement needs approval from the City Engineer and a written agreement. Where the fence crosses the swale, the boards should stop high enough for water to pass, and posts should stay out of the lowest point when possible. Fencing that dams a swale can flood your yard or the one next door in the first big storm.

faqs.q: How long does a wood privacy fence last in Tennessee?
faqs.a: There is no single answer, because it depends mostly on the posts and on the care the fence gets. Posts rated for ground contact and set so water drains away from them make the biggest difference. A fence that gets stained once it dries, stays clear of mulch and soil, and gets checked for loose boards now and then will outlast one that is left alone. Murfreesboro sun and humidity work on every fence, so plan on some upkeep.

faqs.q: What happens to my yard during fence installation?
faqs.a: Expect some wear along the fence line. Post holes produce a pile of clay and rock that has to go somewhere, and the path in and out of the yard sees traffic. Tennessee 811 marks public utility lines, but not private ones like sprinkler lines, landscape lighting, or buried pet containment wire, so flag those before the fence installation crew arrives. Ask where the spoils will go and whether hauling them away is part of the bid.
